blocks.intro: Not all leaks announce themselves. If something feels off, it probably is:

tiles.body: A bill that jumps with no change in how you use water often means water is going somewhere you can't see.

tiles.h3: Stains, Bubbling Paint or Soft Spots
tiles.body: Water stains on ceilings, bubbling paint on walls or soft spots in the floor point to a leak behind the surface.
A damp, musty smell or mold with no obvious cause often traces back to a slow leak.
Hearing water run when every fixture is off is a strong sign of a leak in a supply line.

blocks.intro: From a dripping trap to a split line inside a wall:

steps.body: Faucets, shutoff valves, supply lines and traps under sinks and behind toilets. See [faucet repair](/highland-park/faucet-installation-repair).
Leaks inside walls, ceilings and floors. We locate them with as little opening up as possible.
Leaking supply lines, drain lines and connections in basements and crawl spaces.

blocks.h2: Why Leaks Start in Highland Park Homes
blocks.intro: Nearly half of Highland Park homes were built before 1960, often with galvanized water lines, cast iron drains and older copper. These materials wear out slowly, until a small leak turns into a bigger repair.

items.body: Galvanized pipe corrodes from the inside. Over decades it narrows, weakens at the threads and starts to leak, often at joints inside walls.
Older copper can develop pinhole leaks, and old fittings and shutoff valves wear out. A valve that won't close all the way is a leak waiting to happen.
Long Lake County winters add freeze damage to the list. A spigot line that froze in January may not leak until spring. See [burst pipe repair](/highland-park/burst-pipe-repair).

blocks.h2: Leak Questions From Highland Park Homeowners

items.q: How do I know if I have a hidden water leak?
items.preview: Turn off all fixtures and watch your meter. If it moves, you likely have a leak.
items.answer: Turn off every fixture and check your water meter. If the meter keeps moving, water is going somewhere. Other signs include a higher water bill, stains, bubbling paint, soft floors and a musty smell.

items.q: Can you find a leak without tearing up walls?
items.preview: Usually. We narrow down the location first so any opening is small.
items.answer: In most cases we can narrow down the location before opening anything, so any opening is small and targeted. We'll show you where we think the leak is and why before we cut.

items.q: Should I repair a leak or replace the pipe?
items.preview: One leak on sound pipe is a repair. Repeat leaks on old pipe may mean replacing the section.
items.answer: A single leak on otherwise sound pipe is usually a repair. If the pipe is old galvanized steel or keeps leaking in new places, replacing the section can save you from repeat repairs. We'll explain both options.

items.q: How much does leak repair cost?
items.preview: It depends on location and access. You get a flat-rate price before any work begins.
items.answer: It depends on where the leak is, how easy it is to reach and what the pipe or fixture needs. We give you a flat-rate price before any work begins.
